column4: After 56:86 challenges those claiming they owe no recompense, this ayah demands that they return the departing soul if truthful; تَرْجِعُونَهَا makes ر د د the test of that claim.
God recompenses workers by the best they did, adds from His bounty, and provides without account, joining appraised work to payment beyond a curtailed measure.
A believer who works righteousness enters the Garden and is provided there without account, a close parallel to the section's unmeasured wage.
The blessed remain in the Garden through an عَطَاءً غَيْرَ مَجْذُوذٍ, an uncut gift that states without م م ن wording what the section hears in غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ.
The declaration that God's provision has no exhaustion directly parallels a reward whose amount is neither cut down nor used up.
Those who purchase magic know that its buyer has no خَلَاقٍ in the Hereafter, and the ayah condemns the price for which they sold themselves; measured share and ruinous valuation meet explicitly.
People consume their خَلَاق as earlier peoples consumed theirs and end with void works, showing an allotted worldly share spent without retaining final value.
God is قَائِمًا بِٱلْقِسْطِ and declares His unique divinity with the witnesses, joining the ق و م field to the maintenance of exact justice.
The command to be قَوَّامِينَ بِٱلْقِسْطِ requires testimony against self or kin and refuses to let wealth or poverty distort the appraisal.
Believers must stand firmly as just witnesses and not let hatred cause an inequitable judgment, bringing ق و م into the practice of the section's just measure.
إِنِ ٱلْحُكْمُ إِلَّا لِلَّهِ reserves judgment to God and then calls exclusive worship ٱلدِّينُ ٱلْقَيِّمُ, bringing حكم, د ي ن, and ق و م together in their rule-and-uprightness senses.

The command to set one's face to the dīn invokes the fitrah upon which God خَلَقَ people and calls it ٱلدِّينُ ٱلْقَيِّمُ, joining creation, proportionate fit, and the semantic range of دِين and ق و م.
The upright book is قَيِّمًا and immediately promises faithful righteous workers a good wage, placing moral straightness and recompense in one ayah.
The recipient of the book in the right hand receives an easy حساب, making the manner of final settlement explicit.
The joyful recipient of the record explains that he expected to meet his حساب, joining present valuation to prior accountability.
The recipient of the other record laments that he did not know what his حساب would be, the stance that leaves the account disastrously unpaid.
The mockers demand that their قِطَّنَا, their allotted portion, be hastened before the Day of Account, turning a measured share into sarcasm about final payment.
Every soul is held for what it earned, and no ransom or equivalent payment is accepted apart from God, combining liability, earnings, and the impossibility of buying off the account.
Each soul earns only against itself, bears no other's burden, and returns to the Lord for disclosure, joining personal earnings to final return.
The human begins as a drop, then is created and proportioned; this repeats the sound formation that precedes the question of resurrection and recompense.
God creates the human from a drop and measures or proportions him, a direct creation-side counterpart to the section's assayed human being.
Those given their record in the right hand read it and are not wronged even by a tiny thread, combining the ledger with minute exactness.
No soul can settle for another on the judgment day and no equivalent ransom is accepted, setting a firm boundary on debt transfer and payment.
The ayah calls the price for which they sold themselves evil: rejection born of envy turns the self into badly valued merchandise.
Those who conceal revelation purchase only a small price and consume fire, so apparent market gain is reassessed as punishment.
People throw the scripture behind them and purchase a small price, which the ayah judges an evil acquisition.
Believers from the People of the Book do not exchange God's signs for a small price and therefore retain their wage with their Lord.
The command not to exchange God's signs for a small price makes faithful judgment the alternative to corrupt valuation.
Selling God's signs for a small price leads people to block His way, exposing the moral cost hidden by the quoted price.
Those who manufacture scripture for a small price receive woe both for what their hands wrote and for what they earned, turning fraudulent production into a debit.
Apostasy through death makes works void in both worlds, a direct case of accumulated labor losing all final assay value.
Denial and murderous opposition leave deeds void in this world and the Hereafter, so no final value remains.
Whoever rejects faith has his work voided and becomes one of the losers in the Hereafter, the result of failed moral assay.
Even the named prophets' works would be void if they associated partners, stating the boundary under which work retains value.
Denying God's signs and the meeting of the Hereafter voids works, and the question says they receive only the recompense of what they did.
The self-claimed service of shrine-tending cannot survive open disbelief; its workers' deeds are declared void.
Those sparing with support and abusive after fear passes have their works nullified by God, so outward participation proves debased.
Association would nullify even the addressee's work and place him among the losers, an explicit warning that the coin of labor can fail completely.
Ruin is pronounced upon the disbelievers and their deeds are led astray, beginning a direct account of lost work.
Because they hate what God sent down, He makes their works void, identifying why the labor in 47:8 loses value.
Following what angers God and hating His pleasure results in works being nullified, another stated cause of failed assay.
Those who disbelieve, bar the way, and oppose the messenger cannot harm God, but their own works are nullified.
Believers are expressly warned not to nullify their works, presenting retained value as something obedience must guard.
Believers must spend before a day on which no trade, friendship, or intercession operates, marking the end of ordinary market remedies.
Spending must occur before the day with neither bargaining nor friendship, so present wealth cannot be offered after the account opens.
The day when neither wealth nor children benefit rejects the two common human measures of worth.
No ransom is accepted from hypocrites or disbelievers; the final liability cannot be discharged with a substitute payment.
The plotters against Abraham are made ٱلْأَسْفَلِينَ, turning their intended mastery into divinely assigned lowness.
The condemned ask to place their human and jinn misleaders underfoot among ٱلْأَسْفَلِينَ, exposing the end-value they now assign their former guides.
The command not to give with a view to obtaining more uses the other م ن ن field to forbid treating generosity as an investment seeking enlarged return.
Receiving the record in the right hand supplies the documentary scene that makes the easy account of 84:8 intelligible.
Receiving the record from behind the back marks the rejected side of the ledger before the call for destruction.
The successful person is handed his record in the right hand and invites others to read it, the visible presentation preceding his statement about حساب in 69:20.
The failed person receives the record in the left hand and wishes it had never been given, setting up his ignorance of the account in 69:26.
Worldly life is made attractive to disbelievers, while God provides the God-fearing without account on resurrection, correcting apparent present value.
God gives provision without account to whom He wills, a non-wage formulation of quantity unbounded by ordinary reckoning.
Mary receives provision from God without account, making unmeasured giving concrete within a sanctuary scene.
Property is something God made قِيَامًا for people, preserving the ق و م sense of that by which life stands rather than merely its assessed price.
People who certify their own purity are corrected: God appraises whom He wills and wrongs no one even by a tiny thread.
God honors the children of Adam, provides them good things, and favors them over much creation, a divine valuation of the human being.
God makes good everything He created and begins human creation from clay, another Quranic statement of sound created workmanship.
After 75:38's created and proportioned human, this ayah asks whether that Maker can raise the dead, carrying formation into final accountability.
Forgiveness and enduring gardens are called the excellent wage of workers, another explicit worker-to-wage formulation.
The faithful rejoice that God does not waste the believers' wage, stating preservation of earned value.
Those who hold to the Book and establish prayer are assured that God does not waste the wage of reformers.
Recorded thirst, fatigue, and effort are justified by the rule that God does not waste the wage of good-doers.
Every expenditure and journey is written so that God may recompense the best of the workers' deeds, joining ledger entry and wage.
Patience is commanded because God does not waste the wage of good-doers, a preservation counterpart to the uncurtailed payment.
Yusuf's earthly establishment illustrates that God does not waste the wage of good-doers, though the payment here begins before the final account.
Joseph links reverence and patience to the principle that God does not waste the wage of good-doers.
The father offers marriage in return for eight years of Moses' service and leaves two more voluntary, specifying a negotiated term of labor after 28:26's hiring proposal.
The command not to exchange God's signs for a small price identifies revelation as something market valuation must not cheapen.
One person sells himself seeking God's pleasure, a positive self-exchange whose value is fixed by its divine object.
Those who purchase disbelief with faith cannot harm God and receive painful punishment, another exchange that reveals its true price only at judgment.
Those given a share of scripture purchase error and wish others to lose the way, spending received value on loss.
The call to fight addresses those who sell the worldly life for the Hereafter and promises a great wage whether slain or victorious.
Witnesses must not exchange their oath for a price even when kin could benefit, preserving truthful valuation in an estate account.
Purchasing distracting speech to mislead others turns expenditure into a humiliating liability.
The Lord decides the disputes of the Children of Israel by His حكم, specifying the knowledgeable and powerful Judge behind the decision.
The answer to rejected exclusive worship is that الحكم belongs to God, the Exalted and Great, reserving final decision to Him.
Whatever people dispute has its حكم with God, and the speaker turns back to Him, joining decision and return.
